summary: Defines a YANG module for NAT functions including NAT44, NAT64, CLAT, SIIT and explicit address mappings, plus network prefix translation.

plainLanguage.summary: NAT swaps address labels. This gives a standard form for setting up all of those swaps.

questions: what is the ietf-nat yang module
how to configure carrier grade nat with netconf
subtitle: A standard YANG data model for configuring and monitoring NAT44, NAT64, CLAT, SIIT, NPTv6 and more.

tldr.problem: Operators run many kinds of address and prefix translators, from home NAT44 to carrier-grade NAT and IPv6 translation, and each vendor configures them differently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ietf-nat YANG module, with NAT instances, policies, address pools, mapping entries, resource limits and notifications. YANG features switch on each translation flavor.
tldr.outcome: Network management tools can configure and monitor many NAT flavors in one common way over NETCONF or RESTCONF. Dual-Stack Lite support is added by a separate extension, RFC 8513.

today: RFC 8512 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text names RFC 8513 as an extension for Dual-Stack Lite.

sections.title: Scope and Terminology
sections.content:
RFC 8512 defines a data model, written in the YANG language, for Network Address Translation (NAT) and Network Prefix Translation (NPT). It covers traditional NAT, which RFC 2663 defines, and Carrier Grade NAT (CGN) from RFC 6888. A CGN is run by a service provider rather than by end users, to make better use of global IP address space.

It also covers NAT64 (RFC 6146), the customer-side translator CLAT (RFC 6877), Stateless IP/ICMP Translation, SIIT (RFC 7915), Explicit Address Mappings, EAM (RFC 7757), IPv6 Network Prefix Translation, NPTv6 (RFC 6296), and Destination NAT.

The RFC defines its own terms. A mapping is the state a translator needs for address or port translation. A dynamic implicit mapping is created as a side effect of a packet such as an initial TCP SYN. A dynamic explicit mapping is created by an explicit request, for example a Port Control Protocol message. A static explicit mapping is created by something like a command-line interface and stays until it is removed. The word NAT in the document means any translation flavor.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC makes one common form for setting up all the different kinds of address swapping. It also agrees on what words like "mapping" mean.

sections.title: Instances, Policies and Scope
sections.content:
The module is designed to cover dynamic implicit mappings and static explicit mappings. Instructing dynamic explicit mappings, for example through the Port Control Protocol, is left to separate documents.

A single NAT device can have multiple NAT instances, each with its own policies, configuration data and mapping tables, and each can be enabled or disabled. An instance can have multiple policies (/nat/instances/instance/policy). How hosts or flows are associated with an instance or policy is not assumed, and classification filters are out of scope.

The module also gives no way to turn on logging or choose what is logged. That is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: One translator box can run several separate NAT jobs, each with its own rules and its own notebook of swaps.

sections.title: Translation Flavors and Features
sections.content:
The supported modes include Basic NAT44, NAPT, Destination NAT, port-restricted NAT, stateful NAT64, SIIT, CLAT, EAM and NPTv6, and several combinations of these. RFC 8513 extends the module for Dual-Stack Lite.

The YANG feature statement marks which data nodes apply to which mode. Table 1 of the RFC lists the features: basic-nat44, napt44, dst-nat, nat64, siit, clat, eam and nptv6.

Some modes need no feature of their own. Port-restricted NAT means supplying port-set-restrict policies to a NAPT or NAT64. Combining NAT with Destination NAT means setting dst-nat-enable. Stateless NAT64 for a prefix is chosen with nat64-prefixes/stateless-enable. A NAT instance can also report its capabilities, such as supported translation modes, protocols, mapping and filtering types, and fragment handling.

The document assumes the NAT behavior recommendations for UDP (RFC 4787), TCP (RFC 5382) and ICMP (RFC 5508) are enabled by default. Timers are specified only for UDP, TCP and ICMP, though other transport protocols such as DCCP can be enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has switches, one for each type of address swapping. You turn on only the switches your box actually does.

sections.title: Pools, Port Sets and Mapping Entries
sections.content:
Blocks of external addresses are provisioned as external-ip-address-pool, and they may be contiguous or not. A single address can be configured to suit a traditional NAT. One or more pools may also be set for Destination NAT (dst-ip-address-pool).

A NAT can assign ports one session at a time or hand out port sets, which can reduce logging volume. With port-allocation-type set to port-range-allocation, a port-set-size can be given. For port-restricted addresses, as in Lightweight 4over6 and MAP-E, two schemes are supported: a simple start and end port range, or an algorithm defined in RFC 7597.

A TCP or UDP mapping entry ties internal source and destination addresses and ports to external ones. An ICMP entry uses the ICMP identifier in place of ports. Each entry has a type (for example dynamic or static), a transport-protocol, and the internal and external source and destination address and port fields. An internal address can be IPv4 or IPv6 so one structure covers NAT44 and NAT64.

A mapping table is kept only for stateful NAT functions. None is kept for NPTv6, which is stateless and transport-agnostic, nor for EAM or stateless IPv4/IPv6 translation. CLAT is stateless only if a dedicated IPv6 prefix is provided.
sections.plainLanguage: Each swap is written in a notebook as "inside address and door number turn into outside address and door number". Stateless swappers do not need a notebook because the rule can be worked out from the address itself.

sections.title: Limits, Notifications and Interface Binding
sections.content:
To suit CGN deployments, the module can limit external ports per subscriber (port-quota), and the state memory for each mapping and subscriber (mapping-limits and connection-limits). Limits can be set independently per transport protocol. A fragments-limit caps the out-of-order fragments a translator handles, to reduce denial-of-service risk. Once a limit is reached, packets that would trigger new mappings or use existing ones are dropped.

Thresholds trigger notifications. high-threshold and low-threshold cover address pool utilization and raise a nat-pool-event. notify-addresses-usage, notify-ports-usage and notify-subscribers-limit raise a nat-instance-event. Notify intervals set the minimum number of seconds between successive notifications, so they are rate-limited.

The external-realm says where the NAT applies. It can be an interface, and the module is extensible to other choices such as a VRF instance. If none is given, the system is assumed to determine the external interface itself. The RFC also compares the module with NATV2-MIB and notes that, unlike the MIB, it allows multiple policies per NAT instance.
sections.plainLanguage: A box can cap how many doors one customer may use and send an alert when it is running low. It also tells the manager which side of the box faces the outside world.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security issues of the translators themselves are left to RFCs 6888, 6146, 6877, 6296 and 7757. The module is meant to be accessed with NETCONF or RESTCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH and TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) can restrict which users may use which operations and content.

All writable data nodes are considered sensitive, because unprotected writes can harm network operations. The RFC lists attacks by someone with access to the NAT. They can set a high or low resource limit to cause a denial of service, or set low thresholds to produce useless notifications. They can also set an arbitrarily high threshold so that notifications are deactivated.

The mapping table holds privacy-sensitive data, which can be misused to track the activity of a host.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger can change the box's settings, they can make it misbehave or stay quiet. The swap notebook also shows who talked to whom, so it must be kept private.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-nat in the IETF XML Registry. It also registered the YANG module name ietf-nat with prefix nat and this namespace in the YANG Module Names registry, referencing RFC 8512.

Appendix A gives non-exhaustive XML examples, such as a traditional NAT44 where a UDP packet from 192.0.2.1 port 1568 is translated to 198.51.100.1 port 15000 with a remaining lifetime of 300 seconds. It also has examples for CGN, NAT64, SIIT, EAM, Destination NAT, CLAT and NPTv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The module got an official name and address in the standards registry, so nobody else can use the same name.
